author: ben_a_adams
content: The issue is charging a flat rate for very entirely different amounts of work; loading a 114 byte proxy costs the same gas as massive 64kB contract even though the time to load them from disk is very different

author: gaxanh
content:
What I mean is avoiding increasing the block gas limit so that we don’t have to keep increasing the cost of other bottlenecked resources. How many bytes of contract code a block can load is a separate question.

> The issue is charging a flat rate for very entirely different amounts of work; loading a 114 byte proxy costs the same gas as massive 64kB contract even though the time to load them from disk is very different
Is the cost of loading contract code supposed to scale linearly or in steps? EIP-2929 suggests that loading 24 kB of data is effectively no different from loading just 32 bytes. If that is the intended model, then a stepwise pricing scheme would seem more appropriate.

author: ben_a_adams
content: The 24kB as flat is so is same as today (currently can only deploy 24kB contracts); in Glamsterdam that limit goes to 64kB which causes the issue we are seeing

author: gaxanh
content:
So, with the current block limits in Glamsterdam, can we already accommodate 64 kB contracts?

If the answer is yes, and the goal is to increase throughput in subsequent hard forks, then the only way to do that without increasing the block limit is to reduce the cost of the resources we specifically want to scale.

That’s all I mean.

author: ben_a_adams
content: And why isn't the number of contracts that can be run per block one of the things we want to scale?

author: ben_a_adams
content: Also contract loading takes away from disk resources for SLOAD and STORE directly also

author: gaxanh
content:
As I said above, if the goal is to increase the number of contracts that can be accessed per block, then the straightforward approach is to reduce their cost.

On the other hand, if code access itself is the bottleneck, why not impose a minimum charge based on the number of bytes accessed, similar to EIP-7623? That seems like it would have less impact on UX.

author: ben_a_adams
content: When you access a contract it loads the full contract; so that's exactly what EIP-7907 is proposing. If the contract is larger than 24kB (max in mainnet at Fuska) then charge gas per byte(ish) beyond that size

author: ben_a_adams
content: It has to add it to the account because you need to know that cost BEFORE the EVM pays the cost and make sure you can pay the gas for it; otherwise you can grief by forcing loads you cannot pay for

author: ben_a_adams
content: Not sure what UX impact it has though since you cannot load contracts currently (pre-Glamsterdam) where the extra charging would start; so it would only be contracts beyond Fuska's limit that are now allowed in Glamsterdam that would be charged extra and the charging would be linear based on byte count over 24kB

author: ben_a_adams
content: tl;dr it proposes every contract deployed already has no extra gas charges

author: gaxanh
content:
But we can’t avoid this indefinitely. Sooner or later, the minimum gas cost will exceed the actual amount of gas that needs to be paid. For example, EIP-8279 uses a dynamic floor for the number of block bytes created, while I’ve also seen another EIP proposing lower costs for warm accesses across multiple blocks.

What we should do is make this consumption transparent and observable to contracts, and I think this is entirely feasible to integrate into EIP-8141.

So the approach I have in mind is: reduce the cost of contract access, impose a floor based on the number of contract-code bytes accessed, and expose this information so that contracts can observe it.

author: gaxanh
content:
> so it would only be contracts beyond Fuska's limit that are now allowed in Glamsterdam that would be charged extra and the charging would be linear based on byte count over 24kB
This is just my linear reasoning here: if contract access costs 3,000 gas after Glamsterdam, and each code word accessed beyond the limit is charged 2 gas, then every 24 kB would cost 1,536 gas. That would imply that, excluding the code-access component, the base cost of contract access is only 1,464 gas?

If that’s actually the intended accounting, then perhaps we should use that number as the basis for reducing the contract-access cost, and charge for all code bytes accessed. 24 kB contracts would effectively see the same overall cost as today, while smaller contracts would pay less.
